title: Fast, parallel, three-dimensional rearrangement of atom arrays using superpositions of elementary holograms
authors: D. J. Hoare, P. Dunniece, J. Rodewald, K. K. Voges, M. R. Tarbutt
abstract: Assembling defect-free arrays of neutral atoms requires real-time rearrangement of stochastically loaded optical tweezers. Conventional rearrangement methods shuttle atoms sequentially, whereas high-speed spatial light modulators (SLMs) can move all atoms in parallel, which scales more favorably as the array size grows. For fast parallel rearrangement, the sequence of holograms displayed on the SLM should be computed more rapidly than the SLM refresh rate, and there should be phase continuity between successive holograms to minimize transient intensity fluctuations. We calculate holograms analytically by adding together the complex fields needed to produce each individual trap, and we ramp the phase of each trap linearly as it moves to its target location. Trap positions enter as continuous variables, rather than tied to points on a grid, so the method provides high positioning accuracy. Using a single GPU, we compute each intermediate hologram in 0.284 ms, considerably faster than the SLM refresh time of 0.696 ms, so the rearrangement speed is hardware-limited. In each step, we use the free processing time to iteratively optimize the holograms for equal intensity across the traps, decreasing trap non-uniformity to 1.24% during rearrangement at no cost in total time. Starting from an array of 256 sites loaded stochastically with $^{87}$Rb atoms, we assemble a 100-atom array in under 20 ms with a rearrangement survival probability of 99.31(12)% per atom. This rearrangement increases the temperature of the atoms by 9(3) $μ$K, which is small compared to the trap depth of 480 $μ$K. Our method can also move individual atoms axially, enabling transport in different planes. We demonstrate this capability with a rearrangement protocol where one set of atoms leapfrogs over another.
summary: This paper presents a novel, high-speed method using Superposition-of-Elementary-Holograms (SEH) to reconfigure arrays of neutral atoms trapped by optical tweezers. By calculating holograms faster than the hardware refresh rate, the authors achieved rapid, parallel rearrangement of atom arrays with high fidelity. This advancement is critical for scaling up quantum simulations and quantum computing experiments based on neutral atoms.
main_problem: The core challenge is achieving fast, parallel, and high-fidelity three-dimensional rearrangement of defect-free arrays of neutral atom traps.
main_result: The authors successfully assembled a 100-atom array in under 20 ms with a high survival probability of 99.31% per atom, demonstrating speed limited by the hardware refresh rate.
method: They employ a Superposition-of-Elementary-Holograms (SEH) method combined with Linear Phase Interpolation (LPI) to compute the required holographic phase masks rapidly.
model_or_system: The system involves neutral atoms trapped by optical tweezers generated using high-speed Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs). The method treats trap positions and fields as continuous variables, allowing for precise, parallel manipulation.
key_observables: Rearrangement survival probability (99.31%), trap non-uniformity (reduced to 1.24%), and the time taken for assembly (< 20 ms).
important_parameters: SLM refresh rate (0.696 ms), GPU computation time (0.284 ms), and the trap depth (480 µK).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the SLM only modulates the phase, and the speed is ultimately limited by the SLM's physical refresh rate.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the I-SEH rearrangement protocol steps, from stochastic loading to final defect-free array assembly, alongside fluorescence images of the initial and final states.
paper_structure: The paper details the I-SEH algorithm, comparing its computational scaling against FFT-based methods, presenting the full protocol implementation on Rb atoms, and demonstrating 3D transport capabilities.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering bottleneck in quantum simulation platforms by providing a method to rapidly reconfigure complex atomic arrays, which is crucial for scaling up quantum simulation and quantum information processing.
